title: ‘The eels were climbing out of the water to die’: why did every fish in this idyllic lake perish overnight?
summary:
Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain today

Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain today Steve Rose Thu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 06.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen Alistair and Diane Gould bought Furnace Brook in 2013, they had big plans. It was an idyllic spot: a stream-fed fishing lake nestled in a secluded valley in the High Weald, East Sussex, surrounded by woodland and fields. “People loved to come fishing here because it’s so beautiful,” says Diane. “Some of them had been coming for so many years that they got to know the individual fish.” Diane moved here from Kent in 2000, when Furnace Brook was owned by a distant relative. Her two younger sons, then 10 and 14, flourished. They would chat to the anglers about the fish they were catching and throwing back in, and sell them bacon sandwiches. Her elder son, Simon, moved from London to join them in 2006 and became a keen angler himself, and then the fishing manager, or bailiff, looking after the fish and the landscape around the lake. View image in fullscreen Ed, a local angler, at Furnace Brook. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian Diane, who is 68, and Alistair, 69, met in 2008. After Diane’s relative died, they decided to buy the property. Alistair, an ecological consultant with a background in low-carbon design , had drawn up a plan to restore the entire ecosystem of the eight-hectare (20-acre) site. But two years ago, their plans were blown out of the water. On the morning of 20 June 2024, Alistair and Simon walked down to the lake and noticed dead fish floating on the surface. “We looked at it and thought: ‘This is a bit odd,’” says Alistair. On further inspection, almost everything in the 2.4-hectare lake was dead. “It brings tears to my eyes,” says Diane. There were at least 15 species of fish in the lake, she adds: carp, tench, bream, roach, trout and some large eels. “You get a sort of relationship with them, as living beings.” The larger fish even had names. “It was very traumatic for us all,” Alistair continues. “Obviously for nature directly, but also seeing all these fish on the surface and the fact that Simon has been a fishery bailiff here for 15-plus years and these are his babies, and he’s just seeing them all curl up and die.” View image in fullscreen Massacre … 15 trailer-loads of dead fish were removed from the lake. Photograph: Courtesy of Furnace Brook Diane continues: “More than 2,000 fish were dead. Plus, the ones we don’t know about that sank to the bottom. The eels were climbing out of the lake to die.” Eels are pretty hardy, says Alistair; they can even travel over land if they need to. To see them gasping and dying on the banks was heartbreaking. “It was apocalyptic.” At first, the Goulds thought it must be their fault, that they had mismanaged the fish stocks somehow. But when Alistair walked to the top of the lake, he saw that Clippenham stream, which feeds the lake, was also full of dead fish. “That’s when I twigged: ‘This isn’t us. There’s something else going on.’” It seemed clear to him that pollution was coming from somewhere upstream. “All down the stream, our friends were finding dead fish: lamprey, brown trout, freshwater mussels,” says Diane. The stream runs to the Pevensey Levels on the south coast, where water is extracted for drinking and agriculture. View image in fullscreen ‘The eels were climbing out of the lake to die.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Furnace Brook They immediately called the Environment Agency (EA), the body responsible for the “protection and enhancement” of the environment in England, which visited two days later and declared it a Category 1 incident , the most severe kind, meaning it had “a serious, extensive or persistent impact on the environment, people or property”.
